question: Your chest X-ray report lands in the app before the doctor calls. What is it actually telling you?
answer: That something is wrong. 'Unremarkable' is the good news: nothing worth a remark. 'Impressive' is the bad news: a large, striking finding. 'Occult' only means hidden. In a 2022 survey of 215 adults at the Minnesota State Fair, many read phrases like these the opposite way round.
move: In a medical report, a word that sounds like praise may be a measurement.
ask: Which words in my own test results have I read the wrong way round?

scene.head: Radiology report
scene.title: Findings
scene.body: Heart size is normal and the lungs are unremarkable. The opacity in the left lower lobe is impressive and suggests an occult infection. Follow-up advised.

phrases.why: Written for other doctors. Finding nothing to remark on is the best news a scan can give.
It means striking on the image. Radiologists use it for size and severity, never for praise.

phrases.plain: an infection the X-ray cannot show directly
phrases.why: Occult is just Latin for hidden. Nothing supernatural about it.

scene.ask: One word sounds like praise and is the worst news here. Which?
scene.watch: When a report seems to praise you, ask what the word is measuring.

source: Gotlieb et al., JAMA Network Open, 2022

question: You join a gym in January. This is the clause about leaving, worded the way many are. Where does the gym make its money?
answer: On the months you don't come. The contract never ends unless you end it, and ending it takes a letter. In a study of 7,752 members of three US gyms, people on monthly contracts kept paying for over two months, on average, after their last visit.
move: Before you read the price, read how to leave.
ask: What am I still paying for only because leaving takes effort?

scene.head: Membership agreement
scene.title: Term and cancellation
scene.body: This Agreement is subject to a minimum term of 12 months and thereafter renews automatically every month. The Member may cancel only by giving the Club 30 days' written notice.

phrases.text: subject to a minimum term of 12 months
phrases.plain: locked for a full year, whatever happens,
phrases.why: Term sounds like a timetable. It is a lock: twelve payments, used or not.

phrases.plain: never ends unless you end it
phrases.why: Sold as convenience. It makes paying the default, so every forgotten month is income.

phrases.plain: a posted letter and one more month's fee
phrases.why: Each extra step between you and the exit keeps a few more people paying.

scene.ask: One phrase is where the gym makes most of its money. Which?
scene.watch: Before you read the price, find out how you leave. That is where the money is.

question: The back of a moisturiser, the kind you buy without reading. What does it actually promise you?
answer: Almost nothing you can hold it to. The US FDA says 'hypoallergenic' has no federal definition. 'Dermatologist tested' says a test happened, not how it went. And 'up to' is the best result anyone got: in a 2012 FTC study, almost half of readers took an 'up to' figure as what nearly every buyer gets.
move: 'Up to' is a ceiling dressed as a promise.
ask: Which claim did I trust today without asking who checked it?

scene.head: Daily moisturiser · 50 ml
scene.title: For sensitive skin
scene.body: Hypoallergenic. Dermatologist tested. Up to 48h hydration. Fragrance free, with shea butter and glycerin.

phrases.plain: We call it gentle, and no law says what that means
phrases.why: The FDA says the word has no federal definition. It means what the company wants.

phrases.plain: A skin doctor tried it; we don't say what they found
phrases.why: It borrows a doctor's authority without the doctor's verdict.

phrases.plain: 48 hours for our best tester, maybe far less for you
phrases.why: 'Up to' is a ceiling. Most people read it as what they will get.

scene.ask: One of these claims has no legal meaning at all. Which?
scene.watch: On a label, ask who checked each claim, and what exactly they promised.

source: US FDA, Hypoallergenic Cosmetics; FTC, 'Up To' Claims study, 2012
